public_notes.title: Removal And Rebuilding In The Nation’s Account
public_notes.text: The Nation describes Caddo communities across what are now Louisiana, Texas, Arkansas and Oklahoma. Its account traces multiple forced removals, not one journey shared identically by everyone. It distinguishes a treaty signed by northwestern Louisiana Caddo in 1835 from the evacuation of another group from Texas in 1859. The Kadohadacho, Natchitoches and Hasinai confederacies later consolidated geographically. Allotment brought further land losses. The account also emphasizes twentieth-century rebuilding and a continuing Caddo identity. This government profile does not replace the histories of every constituent band.

public_notes.title: Language Continuity And Heritage Protection
public_notes.text: The Nation dates its current language program to August 1, 2022, while describing decades of community preservation work. Its account connects classes and archival work to that longer effort and distinguishes Caddo from related Caddoan languages and Nations. The linked archive is offered to Caddo citizens and descendants; this profile supplies no lessons, recordings or archive access. The Historic Preservation Department separately describes consultation and repatriation responsibilities. These institutions support continuity. Linking them does not promise that every project is stopped, every item returned or language loss reversed.
